title-group.article-title: Comparison of Efficacy and Safety of Romosozumab versus Denosumab for Treatment of Postmenopausal Osteoporosis: A Meta-analysis

abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Two common molecular-targeted drugs used for treating postmenopausal osteoporosis are denosumab (DEN) and romosozumab (ROMO), with the latter being a newly approved drug. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy of DEN and ROMO therapy over 12 months for the management of osteoporosis in postmenopausal patients. The percentage increase in bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine was the primary outcome of interest, while secondary outcomes included bone density changes at the total hip and incidence of clinical or osteoporotic fractures. Two independent reviewers conducted an electronic search on PubMed, Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library until June 2023 to search for randomized controlled trials that studied the clinical efficacy of ROMO or DEN and included those that fulfilled the eligibility criteria. We used Review Manager 5.4 to analyze our data, with an odds ratio for fractures and pooled mean change for BMD. To assess heterogeneity, we used I2 and Chi-square2. P < 0.05 was considered for statistical significance. This review analyzed twelve trials with a total of 22,445 participants. ROMO and DEN were associated with a significant percentage change in BMD. Patients who received ROMO had significantly lower rates of clinical and osteoporotic fractures, but this was not true for those on DEN. Both ROMO and DEN are effective treatments for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women, increasing BMD within a year. A decrease in fracture incidence is more prominent for ROMO therapy.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Osteoporosis is a systemic condition marked by the interaction of intricate molecular pathways that lead to reduced bone mass and weakened bone strength. One of its primary consequences is a decline in bone mineral density (BMD), which results in bones becoming fragile and more prone to fractures. Although osteoporosis affects both men and women, females are generally at a higher risk, especially in the postmenopausal state. During menopause, decrease in estrogen (along with high body mass index and sedentary lifestyle) contributes to bone loss and structural deterioration – resulting in postmenopausal osteoporosis.[1]

Statistically, 30% of postmenopausal women suffer from osteoporosis. Notably, the condition tends to occur 10–20 years earlier in Indians than in Western populations, posing significant health and economic challenges. Despite its high prevalence – affecting one in three women – data on postmenopausal osteoporosis and its independent predictors remain limited. Identifying common risk factors is essential for developing targeted strategies to manage and mitigate the impact of osteoporosis.[2]

Currently, two main categories of medications are available for managing primary osteoporosis. The most frequently prescribed medications for treating bone loss are Bisphosphonates (BPs) and the receptor activator for the nuclear factor κB-ligand (RANKL) inhibitor denosumab (DEN). On the other hand, teriparatide (PTH-1-34) and aloparatide are prescribed less often.[34] Another drug called romosozumab (ROMO) inhibits sclerostin and has the dual effects of promoting bone growth and reducing bone resorption.[5]

The RANK system, comprised of its ligand (RANKL) and osteoprotegerin (OPG), is necessary for bone remodeling. RANKL binds to RANK, triggering osteoclast precursor cell differentiation and osteoclast activity. OPG balances the effects of RANKL.[6] Imbalances in the expression of RANKL/OPG can lead to bone diseases like osteoporosis.[7] The antiresorptive therapies currently utilized to prevent or treat metabolic bone diseases work by altering the expression of RANKL/OPG.[8]

DEN (AMG-162) is a type of human monoclonal immunoglobulin G2 antibody that is highly specific and has a strong affinity for human RANKL. This antibody effectively blocks the binding of RANK to RANKL, resulting in decreased bone turnover and increased bone mass.[9] Meanwhile, RANKL is also crucial for the growth of T-cells and the functioning of dendritic cells.[1011] Inhibiting its action may impact the immune system, potentially leading to susceptibility to infections or malignancies.[12]

ROMO is an anti-sclerostin that enhances bone formation while preventing bone resorption. It has been recommended by the Endocrine Society for severe osteoporosis and a high fracture risk in postmenopausal women. It should be taken for up to 1 year to lower the risk of fractures. After finishing the course, antiresorptive therapies should be continued to maintain bone density and prevent future fractures.[13]

This review examines how effective DEN and ROMO are for treating postmenopausal osteoporosis. While previous reviews have separately assessed the two drugs,[141516] this meta-analysis focuses on comparing their effectiveness and safety.

sec.title: MATERIALS AND METHODS
sec.p: Our approach to conducting this systematic review was based on rigorous adherence to the “Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses” declaration and the “Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions.” These guidelines ensure that our research is conducted with the highest level of integrity, transparency, and accuracy.[1718]

sec.title: Literature search strategy
sec.p: Two independent reviewers searched PubMed, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and Cochrane Library databases until June 4, 2023. We specifically looked for studies that examined the effectiveness of DEN and ROMO in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. To find relevant studies, we utilized appropriate keywords like “denosumab,” “romosozumab,” “postmenopausal,” and “osteoporosis” and combined them using “OR” or “AND” operators. This meta-analysis was not restricted by language or publication date. When differing opinions arose, the two authors worked together to find a resolution through discussions. If necessary, a third author was consulted for additional input.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Publications short-listed after the electronic database search were included in this review if they fulfilled the following criteria:

list-item.p: The study should include postmenopausal women with osteoporosis
The study had to compare the drug in question (DEN or ROM) with either a placebo (placebo control) or another antiosteoporosis drug (active control) at approved doses
The follow-up period had to be at least 12 months
The study had to be a randomized controlled trial (RCT)

The study should determine the effectiveness of DEN, ROMO, or both in increasing BMD and reducing fractures over the course of the study. The meta-analysis included studies or subgroups within trials where subjects were given DEN 60 mg every 6 months or ROMO 210 mg every month.

sec.p: Publications that did not meet the criteria for inclusion in the research were removed.

Search results were added to a spreadsheet on Microsoft Excel 2010 (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington), and duplicate publications were removed. Two reviewers assessed the titles and abstracts of the remaining articles independently. Ineligible studies were then removed, and any differences in judgment were investigated in full text. To ensure accuracy, a third investigator confirmed the eligibility judgments. In addition, we searched for any additional pertinent research in the reference lists of the studies that were included. Our study selection algorithm is described in Figure 1.

caption.p: PRISMA flow diagram for systematic review

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: Two authors extracted relevant data from each RCT independently using a standardized form. General details such as author(s), journal, study methods, and sample size were included. In addition, they documented methodological data such as inclusion criteria, treatment duration, dose, research quality, and limitations. They also recorded baseline characteristics and outcomes, and if required, they contacted the writers to fill up any gaps in data.

sec.title: Study outcomes
sec.p: In order to evaluate the treatment’s effectiveness, we analyzed two important factors: the increase in BMD (%age) after 12 months of treatment at the lumbar spine and total hip and the occurrence of clinical and osteoporotic fractures throughout the study. Osteoporotic fractures can happen in the spine, hip joint, or proximal femur, including low-level stress fractures.

sec.title: Quality assessment of studies
sec.p: The “risk of bias” (RoB) for any study taken for review was evaluated by two reviewers using the “modified Cochrane RoB tool.”[19] The RoB was categorized as “low,” “high,” or “unknown” based on various factors such as “randomization sequence generation, allocation sequence concealment, blinding, selective outcome reporting, and other forms of bias.” The criterion with the highest risk determined the overall RoB rating. Publication bias was estimated by studying a funnel chart.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: After retrieving the data, we utilized “Review Manager Version 5.4 (Copenhagen, Denmark: The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020)” to analyze it. To examine fractures, we used odds ratios (ORs), while for BMD data, we used pooled mean change. We used the I2 statistic in order to ascertain the degree of heterogeneity present in the data. The fixed effect model was used if the I2 < 50. A random-effect methodology was used otherwise. However, if the data were inconsistent, we relied on the P value as a benchmark. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Grading of evidence
sec.p: We used the GRADE pro-GDT software (https://gradepro.org/) to assess the quality of evidence. The software helped us determine the optimal size for each group, which was 1138 patients. Based on the information gathered, the software classified the quality of evidence as “high,” “moderate,” “low,” or “very low.”[20]

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: We searched systematically until June 4, 2023 and found 1514 records that could meet the criteria for this review. The selection and exclusion process is illustrated in Figure 1. After the removal of repetitive publications, we examined the titles and abstracts of 581 records and found that 467 of those records did not meet the criteria. Reviewers analyzed the full texts of 114 records and found 12 RCTs that involved a total of 22,445 postmenopausal women who were diagnosed with osteoporosis.[212223242526272829303132]

sec.title: Characteristics of enrolled studies
sec.p: Among the included studies, seven compared DEN to a control group,[21222324252627] and five evaluated ROMO.[2829303132] Detailed characteristics and findings of these 12 RCTs are given in Table 1.

sec.p: We included seven trials published from 2009 to 2016 which evaluated the clinical efficacy of DEN involving a total of 11,863 patients.[21222324252627] In two studies, DEN was compared to a placebo,[2225] while in the other five studies, it was compared to BPs (two with alendronate,[2123] one each with zoledronic acid,[24] ibandronate,[26] and risedronate).[27]

We analyzed five RCTs that evaluated ROMO in women with osteoporosis after menopause.[2829303132] These studies were published between 2014 and 2017 and involved 10,582 patients. The study sample sizes varied from 104 to 7180, with four studies lasting 12 months and one lasting 24 months. Among the five studies, three compared ROMO with a placebo,[282931] one each compared it with alendronate[32] and teriparatide.[30]

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: The RoB was analyzed and detailed in Figures 2 and 3. Out of the twelve trials, seven were deemed to have a low RoB, two had a high risk, and three were unclear. Due to the uncertainty surrounding the involvement of the funding institution in the experiments, all other forms of bias were labeled as unclear risks of bias.

sec.title: Percentage change in bone mineral density at the lumbar spine (lumbar spine bone marrow density)
sec.p: To study the impact of ROMO on lumbar spine bone marrow density (LS-BMD) change, RCTs were separated into two categories: “placebo control” and “active control.” The latter involved administering an anti-osteoporotic drug (such as BP or teriparatide) instead of a placebo. In five RCTs, 10,582 patients were studied, with 5288 receiving ROMO treatment and 5294 in the control group. After 12 months of treatment, LS-BMD significantly increased in patients on ROMO, with a mean difference (MD) of 10.62 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 5.54–15.70), P < 0.05. All studies reported a statistically significant increase in LS-BMD at 12 months, and despite high heterogeneity (I2 > 50%) in the analysis, the results can still be considered reliable. In addition, the change in LS-BMD was significantly higher in each subgroup, as shown in Figure 4a.

caption.p: Forest plot for percentage bone mineral density changes in 12 months at the lumbar spine with romosozumab (a) and Denosumab (b); and at the hip joint with Romosozumab (c) and Denosumab (d). LS-BMD: Lumbar spine bone marrow density; TH-BMD: Total hip bone marrow density. SD: standard deviation; CI: confidence interval; IV: inverse variance

sec.p: Only three out of seven trials about DEN provided enough data on the percentage change in LS-BMD for meta-analysis. In all three of these trials, participants in the control group were given BPs. Participants who received DEN (n = 978) showed a meaningful increase in TH-BMD in comparison to those on BPs (n = 952) (MD = 1.91 [95% CI = 1.30–2.52], P < 0.00001; I2 = 69%) [Figure 4b].

To enhance the credibility of these results, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by serially excluding individual trials. This sensitivity analysis demonstrated that the overall effect size remained consistent [Table 2].

sec.title: Percentage change in total hip bone mineral density
sec.p: On meta-analysis, TH-BMD significantly increased among study participants receiving ROMO as opposed to those in control groups of five RCTs (MD = 4.24 [95% CI = 2.84–5.64], P < 0.00001; I2 = 93%), and similar results were seen on subgroup analysis of studies with placebo or active control [Figure 4c]. Similarly, meta-analysis of data from four RCTs involving 2697 participants revealed that TH-BMD after 12 months of treatment was significantly higher for women given DEN (MD = 1.25 [95% CI = 0.96–1.55], P < 0.00001; I2 = 63%) [Figure 4d]. Upon sensitivity analysis, no inconsistencies were observed in the overall effect size [Table 2].

sec.title: Clinical fracture incidence
sec.p: Data for the incidence of clinical fractures were taken from three studies evaluating ROMO, including 5841 patients in the intervention group and 5844 controls. The frequency of new clinical fractures was considerably lowered in patients on ROMO over 12 months compared to those in control groups [Figure 5a] (OR = 0.68 [95% CI = 0.55–0.85], P = 0.0006; I2 = 0%) Moreover, there was no notable heterogeneity among the trials, and the ORs displayed no inconsistencies according to the sensitivity analysis [Table 2].

caption.p: Forest plots for incidence of clinical fracture (a and b) and osteoporotic fracture (c and d), with romosozumab (a and c) and Denosumab (b and d). M-H: Mantel-Haenszel; CI: Confidence interval

sec.p: For studies on DEN, the data on clinical fracture incidence came from seven trials, encompassing 5950 patients in the intervention group and 5913 controls. Patients on DEN had a lower incidence of clinical fractures compared to those in the control group; however, the difference was not statistically significant (P > 0.05) [Figure 5b] (OR = 0.89 [95% CI = 0.76–1.04], P = 0.13; I2 = 11%).

sec.title: Osteoporotic fracture incidence
sec.p: Amongst the trials included in this study, three studies each published data regarding the incidence of osteoporotic fractures for REMO, and four studies for DEN. Incidence of osteoporotic fractures was significantly lower in patients who received REMO for 12 months compared to controls [Figure 5c] (OR = 0.67 [95% CI = 0.52–0.86], P = 0.002; I2 = 0%). However, the risk of osteoporotic fractures among patients on DEN was not significantly different than those in the control group [Figure 5d] (OR = 0.74 [95% CI = 0.27–2.06], P = 0.56; I2 = 80%). The sensitivity analysis of this outcome is summarized in Table 2.

sec.title: Risk of publication bias
sec.p: We created a funnel plot to analyze clinical fracture incidence in seven DEN trials and three ROMO trials. After visually inspecting the plots, it was determined that there was no significant risk of publication bias [Figure 6a and b].

caption.p: Funnel plot for the incidence of clinical fracture in the trial on (a) Denosumab and (b) romosozumab

sec.title: GRADE analysis of outcomes
sec.p: According to the GRADE Pro GDT analysis in this review, the evidence quality for fracture incidence (both clinical and osteoporotic) was rated as “High” for ROMO and “Moderate” for DEN. As for an increase in BMD at the lumbar spine and total hip, the evidence quality was graded as “Moderate” for ROMO and “Low” for DEN. sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: After conducting a thorough analysis of 12 RCTs, including seven on DEN and five on ROMO, we found that women with postmenopausal osteoporosis experienced a significant increase in BMD in the lumbar spine and total hip when treated with either ROMO or DEN. Moreover, patients who received ROMO or DEN had a much lower incidence of fractures compared to those who did not receive treatment.

The primary endpoint of nine out of twelve trials included in this review was a change in BMD at the lumbar spine or total hip. After analyzing the results of the trials reviewed, it was found that both ROMO and DEN improved BMD in the lumbar spine and total hip significantly. However, the increase in BMD was higher for ROMO than for DEN [Figure 4]. Qualitatively, the evidence for ROMO was rated “Moderate,” while the evidence for DEN was rated “Low” [Table 2].

The BMD increase is influenced by three factors: the early closure of the bone remodeling period, a successive increase of bone mineralization, and ongoing modeling-based bone formation.[3334] The proportions of the “anabolic window” are affected by the transition of bone metabolism markers during bone remodeling, where the difference between bone formation and resorption markers plays a crucial role.[35] DEN suppresses bone resorption while inhibiting new bone formation, resulting in bone remodeling. On the other hand, ROMO increases bone formation while simultaneously decreasing osteoclast activity. This leads to a broader anabolic window and has a significant impact on the process of improving bone density. New research shows that ROMO has a stronger influence on bone modeling than remodeling, which would make it more successful in improving BMD.[3637] Results from our meta-analysis also support this theory.

In this meta-analysis, three trials focused on fracture incidence as the primary outcome, while others examined clinical or osteoporotic fractures as secondary outcomes or adverse effects. Postmenopausal women on ROMO therapy for 12 months had significantly fewer clinical fractures, including osteoporotic fractures (based on “high” quality evidence). A reduction in the risk of vertebral fractures at 12 months and nonvertebral fractures at 24 months was shown to be associated with ROMO treatment, according to the findings of a meta-analysis conducted by Singh et al.[38] The study showed that vertebral fractures were less likely to occur with an OR of 0.51 (95% CI of 0.40–0.65, p0.00001; I2 = 86%). Nonvertebral fractures also had lower odds with an OR of 0.78 (95% CI of 0.66–0.92, P = 0.003; I2 = 0%). The research by Liu et al. found that ROMO greatly reduced the occurrence of vertebral fractures over 24 months.[16] On the other hand, Hernandez et al. found that while ROMO was effective in lowering the risk of vertebral fractures, it had no effect on the risk of fractures in locations other than the vertebrae.[39]

After analyzing data from various trials on DEN, it was found that there was no significant decrease in the occurrence of clinical or osteoporotic fractures among patients. This is consistent with other systematic reviews as well.[1540] It is possible that over-suppressing bone turnover could cause microdamage accumulation, leading to “frozen bone” and contributing to the lack of fracture risk reduction.[41] Another possibility is that the increase in BMD over a short period of time was not sufficient to lower the risk of fractures.

To ensure the accuracy of our findings, we conducted a thorough sensitivity analysis of all the results included in this evaluation. We took into consideration various factors that could affect the findings, such as the subjects’ ages, previous treatment with BPs, and whether the control group received a placebo or real medication. However, after removing the effects of individual trials, we found no significant differences. We also examined the funnel plot, which showed no evidence of severe publication bias. It is worth noting that the funnel plot analysis may not be entirely accurate since the meta-analysis only included a limited number of trials.

We conducted a comprehensive assessment and used GRADE Pro GDT guidelines to analyze the data. The GRADE system helps ensure high-quality evidence, and in our review, we found important outcomes (such as fracture incidence and changes in BMD) to be of high or moderate rating. We are confident that adding higher-quality RCTs would not significantly change the estimate or our confidence in the data.[20]

Our meta-analysis yielded helpful insights, but it had some limitations. Most of the research we analyzed was funded by pharmaceutical companies, which could have influenced outcomes. In addition, we included individuals with osteoporosis from different countries, each with its own diagnostic criteria, leading to clinical diversity.

sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: This systematic review provided reliable evidence on the effectiveness of ROMO and DEN in treating osteoporosis in women after menopause. The meta-analysis established that treatment with both drugs led to a substantial improvement in bone density within 12 months. In addition, ROMO was found to lower the occurrence of clinical and osteoporotic fractures significantly, where no such effect was observed with DEN.
